While waste-based fuel pathways offer both economic advantages and lower environmental impacts, the limited availability and distributed nature of waste feedstocks pose challenges for scaling up biorefinery infrastructure. On the other hand, alternative fuels such as electro-ammonia from green hydrogen, RD or bio-oil from woody biomass via CFP, and DME from woody biomass gasification can also reduce emissions by at least 85% and decrease CAPs relative to emission standards. Furthermore, green hydrogen and woody biomass are scalable because their feedstock is more abundant, making them attractive options for biorefinery development. However, the MFSP of e-fuels like electro-ammonia and electro- methanol remain higher, potentially limiting their economic feasibility for commercialization, 19 even with the inclusion of LCFS credits. Future research should explore additional alternative fuel pathways and diverse feedstocks to offer a more comprehensive assessment of TEA and LCA, considering scalability and practical applications in freight rail locomotives. 20 3 RAIL ENGINE EFFICIENCY, COMPATIBILITY, AND EMISSIONS In the United States, the freight rail sector is primarily powered by diesel-electric locomotives, which employ diesel engines to power an electric generator that sends electricity to motors powering multiple axles of the locomotive. The engines that power these locomotives are large, four-stroke diesel engines. An example is the 12-cylinder Wabtec Evolution, which is a 45,000-hp, turbocharged V12 locomotive engine used for long-haul freight rail applications. Each cylinder of this engine has a displacement of 15.7 L, and a 250-mm bore. In comparison, Class-8 truck engines have a total displacement of 13–16 L and have nominally 130–140-mm bores. The locomotives used in freight rail applications across North American Class-1 railroads are all diesel engines and are designed to maximize efficiency and minimize criteria emissions using ultra-low sulfur diesel with a high cetane number (cetane number is a measure of a fuel to show how easily any fuel will auto ignite in diesel engines). The EPA sets the U.S. emissions regulations for emissions from newly manufactured and remanufactured locomotives (EPA, 2016). Line-haul locomotives are long-living assets that have useful lifespans of 30 years or more with regular engine rebuilds. Industry feedback has indicated that drop-in replacements and fuel system retrofits for alternative fuels are of interest to meet regulatory requirements globally and customer demands, in addition to OEM (original equipment manufacturer) efforts to design next-generation locomotives. This project considers seven alternative fuels for use in the freight locomotive sector. These fuels range from drop-in replacements for the incumbent ultra-low-sulfur diesel used in current diesel engine systems to fuels that would require significant engine modifications. Alternative fuels such as methanol and ethanol have a near-zero cetane number; instead, they have high research octane numbers (a measure of resistance to auto-ignite or knock in a spark-ignited engine).
